text: The Lugbara are a Central Sudanic ethnic group primarily residing in the West Nile region of Uganda, including the districts of Arua City, Arua, Maracha, Terego, Madi-Okollo, Yumbe, and Koboko, as well as in the adjacent areas of the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) and a small number in South Sudan. They speak the Lugbara language, a Central Sudanic language closely related to that of the Madi, with whom they share cultural similarities. The Lugbara are divided into several dialects—Ayivu, Maracha, Terego, Vurra, and Aringa—that are mutually intelligible. Tribes linguistically related to the Lugbara include the Madi and Kaliko in South Sudan. A distinctive cultural practice is the Cikiri ceremony, held every time a child is born. Historically, the Lugbara were organized into chiefdoms without kingdoms or kings, relying on chiefs as leaders. They formed alliances with neighboring tribes for security and had no standing army; instead, every able-bodied man was considered a soldier, with the duty to protect his village, though it was not permanent. Originally animist, the Lugbara now predominantly follow Christianity, with Islam being another major religion. According to the 2002 Uganda Census, approximately 48.6% are Roman Catholic, 21.4% are Anglican, and 29.1% are Sunni Muslim. They are settled subsistence farmers, with cassava now the traditional staple, though previously millet and sorghum were consumed due to droughts in the 1960s. They cultivate millet, sorghum, legumes, pigeon peas, beans, root crops, groundnuts, Simsim (sesame), chick peas, and sweet potatoes. Chicken, pigs, goats, and cattle (at higher elevations) are also important livestock. Maize is grown for beer production, and tobacco is a key cash crop; emerging cash crops include avocado, pineapple, and mangoes. In 1874, a faction of the Lugbara in the northeastern DRC was known as "The Naked People" because most women did not wear shirts or dresses and were covered with grass skirts or leaves; Lugbara men, who are taller than many Congolese, are skilled hunters using powerful bows with long arrows tipped with fishing hooks. The group straddles the Uganda-DRC border, with the majority living on the DRC side. A collection of Lugbara proverbs has been published, detailing their ethical significance, and the same author has described other traditional customs and society. Notable Lugbara individuals include Dorcus Inzikuru, the 3000-metre steeple chase world champion from Helsinki 2005, Jackson Asiku, the former Commonwealth boxing light-weight champion, John Munduga, an international boxer, and Idi Amin Dada, former Ugandan president known for expelling Asians. The cultural symbol of the Lugbara is a leopard with 300 spots.
